newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unions expect 10,000 for Renault demo.
newsitem.headline: Unions expect 10,000 for Renault demo.

text.p: Trade unions expect 10,000 people to demonstrate at Renault headquarters on Tuesday to press the car maker to scrap plans for cutting nearly 6,000 jobs in Europe, union officials said on Monday.
The protest is scheduled for 1000 GMT on Tuesday, before a meeting between chairman Louis Schweitzer and Renault's European staff works council at 1300 GMT.

"We're going to ask for two things at the meeting -- that Renault reconsider the closure of the Vilvoorde plant (in Belgium), and for the start of negotiations to reduce working hours to preserve jobs under the (French) Robien law," said Emmanuel Couvreur, a spokesman for the CFDT union.

Renault announced on February 27 that it would close the Vilvoorde plant, which employs 3,100 people, in July as part of a programme to reorganise and streamline its European car assembly operations. Last week it also announced plans to eliminate 2,764 jobs in France this year, up from 1,640 job cuts in 1996.
The moves have sparked an uproar not just among workers but also among French and Belgian politicians who say they are appalled by the brutality of the measures and the short notice.
"The demonstration is expected to draw between 4,500 and 5,000 Belgians, about the same number in France, and 50 to 100 workers from Spain," Couvreur said. Some Portuguese workers might also attend.

A spokesman for the Communist-led CGT, the biggest union at Renault, said around 10,000 people were expected on Tuesday. The Belgian contingent would include relatives of Renault employees and workers from firms supplying the Vilvoorde plant.
A convoy of 110 buses was scheduled to leave Vilvoorde on Tuesday before dawn to transport workers to Renault's headquarters in Boulogne-Billancourt on the outskirts of Paris.

Unions have organised work stoppages, marches and protests since the job cuts were announced, but the company and unions give widely differing accounts of the extent to which Renault's 140,000 employees have participated in the labour actions.

Renault is expected to report a loss on its operations of more than two billion francs ($350 million) for 1996 and a total loss of close to six billion francs. Renault , the smallest and weakest of Europe's six mass car manufacturers, says the measures are necessary due to growing competition in the sluggish European car market.

"Through this financial strategy of cost reductions and job cuts, Renault is downsizing...which can only lead to progressive weakening, putting its very existence at risk," the CFDT union said in a statement.

The unions have also called on workers at Renault's plants to stage strikes lasting one hour or longer on Tuesday to support the protest. Workers at the Vilvoorde plant have been on strike since the closure was announced.

Renault's stock, which rallied sharply on the cost-cutting measures, has been slipping on concerns about the pressure mounting on the company. Renault shares closed down 0.6 percent at 138.90 francs on Monday.
